name: True Airspeed from Density Ratio
description: Converts calibrated airspeed to true airspeed by multiplying by the square root of the sea-level to actual air density ratio. As air thins with altitude, true airspeed exceeds the calibrated (indicated) value.
notes: This simplified relation ignores compressibility and instrument or position error, so it is most accurate at low speeds and moderate altitude. Densities must share the same unit.

name: True Airspeed from Mach Number
description: Computes true airspeed as the Mach number times the local speed of sound, where the speed of sound is the square root of the specific heat ratio times the specific gas constant times the static temperature. Higher temperature raises the speed of sound and thus true airspeed.
notes: Temperature must be absolute (kelvin), not Celsius, and is the static air temperature at altitude. The variable labeled g here is the specific heat ratio (about 1.4 for air), not gravity.

name: Density Altitude (Approx)
description: Estimates density altitude by adding to the pressure altitude a correction of about 118.8 feet per degree Celsius that the outside air temperature exceeds the standard temperature at that pressure altitude. It gives the altitude the air density corresponds to in a standard atmosphere.
notes: The 15-0.00198*PA term is the ISA standard temperature in Celsius at that pressure altitude. Inputs are in feet and Celsius; this is a linear approximation to the exact density-altitude relation.

name: Pressure Altitude (Approx)
description: Estimates pressure altitude by adjusting the field elevation for the difference between the standard sea-level pressure of 1013.25 hPa and the current altimeter setting, at about 30 feet per hectopascal. It gives the altitude in the standard atmosphere matching the ambient pressure.
notes: Below standard pressure (QNH), the correction adds height; above it, it subtracts. Inputs use feet and hPa; the 30 ft per hPa factor is a near-surface approximation.

name: Rate of Climb (Excess Power)
description: Computes the maximum rate of climb from the excess thrust over drag times airspeed, divided by weight. It expresses how fast an aircraft can gain altitude using the specific excess power available.
notes: Assumes a small climb angle so thrust and drag act along the flight path; forces are in newtons and the result is in m/s. It gives the instantaneous, steady rate at that speed.

name: Climb Gradient Angle
description: Computes the steady climb angle as the arcsine of the excess thrust over drag divided by weight. It gives the flight path angle an aircraft can sustain in a straight climb at that thrust setting.
notes: Requires thrust above drag and the ratio at most 1, or the arcsine is undefined. Forces in newtons; the result is in radians. Assumes steady, unaccelerated climb.

name: Turn Radius
description: Computes the radius of a level, coordinated turn from the true airspeed, gravity, and load factor. A higher load factor (steeper bank) tightens the turn, while higher speed widens it.
notes: Requires a load factor above 1; at n=1 the turn radius is infinite (wings level). Assumes a coordinated level turn. Airspeed in m/s gives radius in meters.

name: Turn Rate
description: Computes the angular turn rate of a level, coordinated turn from gravity, load factor, and true airspeed. A higher load factor speeds the turn while higher airspeed slows it.
notes: Requires a load factor above 1; at n=1 the turn rate is zero. Assumes a coordinated level turn. Result is in radians per second with airspeed in m/s.

name: Load Factor from Bank Angle
description: Computes the load factor in a level, coordinated turn as one over the cosine of the bank angle. It gives the multiple of normal weight the wings must support to hold altitude at that bank.
notes: Bank angle is in radians and must stay below 90 degrees, where the load factor grows without bound. Valid only for a level, coordinated turn with no climb or descent.

name: Stall Speed in Turn
description: Computes the stall speed in a turn as the level-flight stall speed times the square root of the load factor. The increased load in a banked turn raises the speed at which the wing stalls.
notes: The load factor is dimensionless (n=1/cos(bank) for a level turn), and stall speed scales with its square root. Result shares the unit of the input stall speed.

name: Standard Rate Turn Bank Angle
description: Computes the bank angle required for a given turn rate at a given true airspeed, as the arctangent of the turn rate times airspeed divided by gravity. Faster aircraft need a steeper bank to hold the same turn rate.
notes: Turn rate is in radians per second (a standard-rate turn is 3 deg/s, about 0.0524 rad/s) and airspeed in m/s. The result is in radians and assumes a coordinated level turn.

name: Crosswind Component
description: Computes the crosswind component as the wind speed times the sine of the angle between the wind and the runway heading. It gives the part of the wind acting across the runway, which matters for takeoff and landing limits.
notes: The angle is in radians, measured between the wind direction and the runway. At 90 degrees the full wind is crosswind; the complementary cosine term gives the headwind component.

name: Headwind Component
description: Computes the component of the wind blowing straight down the runway by projecting the wind vector onto the runway heading, V times cos(theta). A positive result is a headwind that shortens takeoff and landing rolls; a negative result is a tailwind.
notes: theta is the angle between the wind and the runway centerline in radians (0 = pure headwind). At theta = pi/2 the headwind is zero, and beyond that the value turns negative, indicating a tailwind.

name: Ground Speed (Wind Triangle)
description: Solves the wind triangle for ground speed using the law of cosines, combining true airspeed and wind speed separated by the angle between the wind and the desired track. The result is the actual speed over the ground.
notes: theta is the angle between the wind vector and the intended track in radians. This gives magnitude only; the required heading (wind correction angle) must be found separately.

name: Wind Correction Angle
description: Gives the angle the aircraft must crab into the wind to hold the desired track, from asin(Ws*sin(wa)/TAS). It balances the crosswind component against true airspeed so the ground track stays on course.
notes: wa is the angle between the wind and the desired track in radians. The formula requires Ws*sin(wa) to be no larger than TAS; otherwise the crosswind exceeds airspeed and no valid correction exists.

name: Glide Distance
description: Estimates the horizontal distance an unpowered aircraft can glide from a given altitude by multiplying the height by the glide ratio, h times LD. A glide ratio of 17 means 17 meters forward per meter of descent.
notes: Assumes a steady glide at the best lift-to-drag ratio in still air, ignoring wind. Head or tail winds shorten or extend the actual reach.

name: Best Glide Speed
description: Gives the airspeed for maximum lift-to-drag ratio, where glide range is greatest, from the wing loading and the drag polar coefficients. It is the speed that minimizes the glide angle in unpowered flight.
notes: Uses a parabolic drag polar Cd = Cd0 + K*CL^2 and requires consistent SI units (W in newtons, S in square meters). Weight, air density, and configuration all shift this speed.

name: Minimum Sink Speed
description: Gives the airspeed that produces the slowest rate of descent (minimum sink), which maximizes time aloft in a glide. It occurs at the maximum of CL^1.5/CD and is lower than the best-glide speed.
notes: Based on a parabolic drag polar; the factor 3 distinguishes it from best-glide speed. Minimum sink maximizes endurance, not range. Use consistent SI units.

name: Breguet Range (Jet)
description: Estimates the maximum still-air range of a jet aircraft in cruise as V/c times the lift-to-drag ratio times the natural log of the initial-to-final weight ratio. Burning more fuel (larger Wi/Wf) or a higher L/D extends range.
notes: Assumes constant speed, L/D, and thrust specific fuel consumption. c is per second, so keep V in m/s; the result is in meters. Wf must be less than Wi.

name: Breguet Endurance (Jet)
description: Estimates how long a jet can stay airborne on a given fuel load as (1/c) times the lift-to-drag ratio times the natural log of the initial-to-final weight ratio. Unlike range, it does not depend on cruise speed.
notes: Assumes constant L/D and thrust specific fuel consumption. With c in per second the result is in seconds; Wf must be less than Wi. Maximum endurance occurs at maximum L/D.

name: Breguet Range (Propeller)
description: Estimates the still-air range of a propeller aircraft as the propeller efficiency divided by brake specific fuel consumption, times L/D, times the natural log of the initial-to-final weight ratio. Higher propeller efficiency and L/D extend range.
notes: Assumes constant efficiency, L/D, and fuel consumption. Here c is per meter (energy-based BSFC form), giving a result in meters; Wf must be less than Wi.

name: Lift Coefficient (from Lift)
description: Back-solves the lift equation for the dimensionless lift coefficient, CL = 2L/(rho*V^2*S). It expresses how much lift the wing generates relative to dynamic pressure and wing area.
notes: V is true airspeed and appears squared, so CL is very sensitive to speed. Use consistent SI units; the result is dimensionless.

name: Power Required (Level Flight)
description: Gives the power needed to overcome drag in steady level flight as drag times airspeed, D times V. This is the power that must be delivered to the airframe to hold speed and altitude.
notes: This is power required to overcome drag, not engine shaft or thrust power; propulsive efficiency losses are not included. Keep D in newtons and V in m/s for a result in watts.

name: Thrust Required (Level Flight)
description: Gives the thrust needed for steady level flight as weight divided by the lift-to-drag ratio, W/LD. In equilibrium lift equals weight and thrust equals drag, so a higher L/D lowers the thrust required.
notes: Valid for unaccelerated level flight where lift equals weight. It equals drag at that condition; climbing or turning raises the required thrust.

name: Chord Reynolds Number
description: Computes the dimensionless Reynolds number based on wing chord, rho*V*ch/mu, comparing inertial to viscous forces in the airflow over the airfoil. It indicates whether the boundary layer tends toward laminar or turbulent flow.
notes: Uses chord length as the characteristic dimension. Keep all inputs in SI units (density in kg/m^3, viscosity in Pa*s); the result is dimensionless.

name: Wing Aspect Ratio
description: Computes the wing aspect ratio as span squared divided by wing area, b^2/S. Higher aspect ratios reduce induced drag and improve gliding efficiency, at the cost of structural weight and roll response.
notes: The b^2/S form works for any planform, not just rectangular wings (for a rectangular wing it reduces to span/chord). The result is dimensionless.

name: Mean Aerodynamic Chord (Tapered Wing)
description: Computes the mean aerodynamic chord of a linearly tapered wing from the root chord and taper ratio. The MAC is the representative chord used for aerodynamic and stability calculations such as locating the center of gravity.
notes: lam is tip chord divided by root chord (0 to 1). Assumes a straight linear taper; at lam = 1 (no taper) the MAC equals the root chord.

name: Takeoff Ground Roll (Approx)
description: Estimates the ground distance to reach liftoff speed under constant acceleration, Vlof^2/(2*acc), from the kinematic relation between speed, acceleration, and distance. It gives the runway length used before the wheels leave the ground.
notes: Assumes a constant mean acceleration and a start from rest. Real rolls vary as thrust and drag change with speed; this is a first-order estimate only.

name: Landing Ground Roll (Approx)
description: Estimates the ground distance to stop from touchdown speed under constant deceleration, Vtd^2/(2*dec), from the kinematic speed-distance relation. It gives the runway length used from touchdown to a full stop.
notes: Assumes a constant mean deceleration to a full stop. Actual braking varies with braking force, aerodynamic drag, and runway condition; this is a first-order estimate.

name: Energy Height (Specific Energy)
description: Computes specific energy (energy height), the total mechanical energy per unit weight expressed as an altitude, h + V^2/(2g). It represents the height the aircraft could reach if all kinetic energy were traded for potential energy.
notes: V is true airspeed. Both terms come out in meters, so the sum is a height, not a literal altitude the aircraft occupies. It ignores drag and thrust during the trade.

name: Load Factor in Pull-up
description: Gives the load factor (g-force) during a level pull-up as 1 + V^2/(g*Rp), the sum of supporting weight plus the centripetal acceleration of the curved path. A tighter radius or higher speed raises the g-load on airframe and crew.
notes: Applies at the bottom of a vertical pull-up where lift supports weight and turns the aircraft. The result is in multiples of g; a value of 1 means unaccelerated flight.

name: Maneuvering (Corner) Speed
description: Gives the corner (maneuvering) speed, the lowest speed at which the wing can reach its maximum load factor before stalling, sqrt(2*nmax*W/(rho*S*CLmax)). It is the speed for the tightest turn without structural overstress.
notes: At this speed full aft stick reaches limit load and stall simultaneously; above it the wing can overstress the airframe, below it the wing stalls first. Use consistent SI units.

name: ISA Temperature (Troposphere)
description: Gives the air temperature at a given altitude in the troposphere under the International Standard Atmosphere, 288.15 - 0.0065*h. It applies the standard sea-level temperature of 288.15 K and a lapse rate of 6.5 K per kilometer.
notes: h is geopotential altitude in meters and the result is in kelvin. Valid only up to the tropopause at about 11000 m, where the temperature stops falling.

name: ISA Pressure (Barometric)
description: Gives the atmospheric pressure at altitude in the troposphere under the International Standard Atmosphere, 101325*(1 - 2.25577e-5*h)^5.25588. It starts from the standard sea-level pressure of 101325 Pa.
notes: h is altitude in meters and the result is in pascals. The exponent embeds the standard lapse rate and gravity, so it is valid only below the tropopause (about 11000 m).

name: ISA Density (Barometric)
description: Gives the air density at altitude in the troposphere under the International Standard Atmosphere, 1.225*(1 - 2.25577e-5*h)^4.25588. It starts from the standard sea-level density of 1.225 kg/m^3.
notes: h is altitude in meters and the result is in kg/m^3. The exponent differs from the pressure formula by one because density also depends on temperature; valid below about 11000 m.

name: Propeller Advance Ratio
description: Computes the propeller advance ratio, the dimensionless ratio of forward airspeed to the product of rotation rate and diameter, V/(nr*D). It characterizes the propeller operating point, analogous to the angle of attack of the blades.
notes: nr is rotations per second (not radians per second or RPM), and D is the full diameter. The result is dimensionless; propeller efficiency curves are plotted against it.

name: Propeller Tip Mach Number
description: Gives the Mach number at the propeller blade tip by combining the forward airspeed with the tip rotational speed vectorially and dividing by the local speed of sound, sqrt(V^2 + (pi*nr*D)^2)/a. It flags when tips approach compressibility limits.
notes: pi*nr*D is the tip rotational speed for rotation rate nr in rev/s and diameter D. Tip Mach numbers approaching 1 cause efficiency loss and noise; keep well below unity.

name: Specific Fuel Consumption
description: Computes specific fuel consumption as the fuel flow rate divided by the thrust or power produced, a standard measure of propulsion efficiency used to compare engines.
notes: Use thrust (giving TSFC, thrust-specific fuel consumption) for jet and turbofan engines, or shaft power (giving PSFC) for turboprop and piston engines; keep the output unit consistent with the quantity chosen. Lower values indicate a more fuel-efficient engine.

name: Rate of Descent (Glide)
description: Estimates the steady-state rate of descent during a power-off glide from the true airspeed TAS and the lift-to-drag ratio LD, using the standard aviation approximation ROD = TAS × 101.3 / (L/D).
notes: The constant 101.3 converts knots to feet per minute (1 kt ≈ 101.3 ft/min) under the small-angle assumption that sink rate equals horizontal speed divided by L/D. A higher L/D or lower airspeed gives a shallower descent.
